newsitem.title: FRANCE: French far-right fights key battle in Provence.
newsitem.headline: French far-right fights key battle in Provence.

text.p: Bruno Megret, number two in France's National Front, stirred little voter enthusiasm on Thursday as he took his bid to haul the far-right into parliament to a picturesque quay-side market in southern Provence.

As Socialist and centre-right candidates also worked the stalls, the market west of Marseille briefly became the battleground for one of the most hotly-disputed seats in the country's May 25-June 1 poll.
The region, dominated by the chemicals and aerospace industries, offers the anti-immigrant Front one of its best chances of winning representation in the National Assembly.

The dapper Megret, the party's business manager and ideologist, said he was sure of repeating, at parliamentary level, his wife's triumph in nearby Vitrolles in April, when she became the Front's fourth mayor.

"Immigration is one of the main issues but not the only one. There is also globalisation, which is causing big unemployment in France, and which is due to international trade and European integration," Megret told Reuters.
"People must chose between the establishment, be it of the left or of the right, and us who represent real change. We propose to fight insecurity, and that's what people got in Vitrolles," he said.

But his conversations with local people did not go much beyond a "Bonjour, how are you, have you had a leaflet?". A roast chicken seller was the most cooperative, complaining business was bad. "That's got to change," Megret replied.
Asked whether he would vote for the Front, after Megret had walked on, the stallholder answered: "You can support the Front without necessarily saying so out loud."
The large number of "don't knows" in opinion polls, and varying estimates of how many voters refuse to admit supporting the Front, clouds forecasts for the key constituency and makes it an open call.

Outgoing Socialist deputy Henri d'Attilio dismissed Megret as a Parisian parachuted in by the Front. "Megret is laughable when he talks about unemployment. He has been sacking staff since the Megret family took power in Vitrolles," said D'Attilio, mayor of Chateauneuf-les-Martigues for the past 26 years.

"I haven't been parachuted here," retorted Megret. "Mr D'Attilio says he is a Provencal but he's the guy bringing in immigrants. I've lived here 10 years now." Candidates ignored each other superbly when their paths crossed.
In Vitrolles itself, anti-Front associations including Ras Le Front (Sick of the Front), highlight rising tension following its election win.
"The Front wants to make Vitrolles, and this constituency, a laboratory for an experiment in government," said Ras Le Front activist Philippe Lamotte.

"The Front's security guards are in and around the town hall and stopping protests and demonstrations. The atmosphere is tense, and our militants are insulted, threatened with death, and physically attacked," he said.

The Front has no seats in parliament now. Its leader Jean-Marie Le Pen won 15 percent of the vote in the 1995 presidential election and it is expected to poll around the same in the general election, but this would entitle it to four seats at the most.

In Orange, just north of Marseille, Front mayor Jacques Bompard makes no bones about the problems facing France: immigration and Europe. "French politicians, instead of defending the interests of the French, are defending those of foreigners," he said.
"They're committing a crime, high treason against the national interests."
